newsitem.title: USA: American pilots ratify new labor contract.
newsitem.headline: American pilots ratify new labor contract.

text.p: The pilots at American Airlines ratified a new five-year labor contract, the airline said Monday, ending months of bitter negotiations and allowing the nation's second largest airline to proceed with a major order for Boeing Co. jets.

American said that 69.3 percent of the pilots approved the contract. The ratification by the Allied Pilots Association's (APA) members removes the threat of a second pilot strike by the union's 9,300 members.

"We are very pleased. It was a very nice, solid ratification. We wanted to have a very solid indication from the membership that they supported it, and we got that in almost every base," said American Airlines President Donald Carty.

The pilots and American Airlines had been in talks to finalize a labor agreement since the current contract ran out August 31, 1994. The recent negotiations were marked by a brief strike in February, intervention by President Clinton and millions of dollars in lost revenues at American, a unit of Fort Worth, Texas-bsaed AMR Corp.

The airline said labor disruptions cut first quarter earnings by $70 million. The company said it may take a "small, additional hit" in the second quarter, but declined to provide a specific forecast.
Under the new five-year contract, pilots will get a 9 percent wage increase and stock options valued at $10 below Monday's average trading price of $93.375.
The deal also includes a compromise on the most hotly contested issue regarding which pilots will fly new jets American plans to buy for its regional jet carrier, American Eagle.

American had wanted American Eagle pilots, who are paid less than APA members, to fly the smaller, regional jets so the company can remain competitive with low-cost carriers. The APA pilots were concerned that the American Eagle pilots would eventually take over their current routes.
The new contract new contract guarantees that furloughed APA pilots will be able to fly the new jets that the carrier is buying for American Eagle.

"I think the majority of the pilots, while they may not have had everything they want in a contract, you seldom do. I think they were ready to get on with the business of rebuilding the airline and providing for some growth in the airline," Carty said.
Union representatives could not be immediately reached for comment.

The contract approval also allows American to proceed with an order for Boeing jets. Under a deal signed last November, American agreed to buy 103 aircraft worth more than $6 billion by the year 2001 and acquired options on 527 more. That order was contigent on the pilots approving the initial labor agreement.

When the pilots rejected the initial tentative wage contract in January, American was forced to delay delivery on at least 14 Boeing jets scheduled for next year. Boeing sold many of the delivery positions it had slated for American.
American said it will make a decision "in the next week or so" regarding the Boeing jet order.
"It won't be exactly the way it was before, we have had some slippage in delivery positions, but we are very anxious to have that not disrupt our momentum," Carty said.
"While the number (of jet orders) isn't likely to change much," the airline may substitute aircraft models, Carty said.
The airline said it also will make a decision about the purchase of regional jets in about 30 to 60 days once the major Boeing contract is finalized.

Although most industry analysts and labor experts had expected the rank-and-file pilots to approve the contract, some investors were cautious since the pilots have rejected deals approved by the union leadership in the past.
In January, the APA members rejected a tentative contract even though the union board had recommended approval.
The pilots went on strike on Feb. 15, but were forced back to work within minutes by a Presidential Emergency Board established by President Clinton to resolve the dispute.
Shares of AMR closed at $94, down $1.125.
